content:
Earlier this year, Apple decided to discontinue the Pro Display XDR entirely. The display hardware was excellent, but it hadn't been updated in years and still cost upwards of $6,000. Apple's current lineup now consists of the Studio Display and the new Studio Display XDR, both of which—while having their own merits—currently only offer 27-inch 5K screens. The XDR version starts at a staggering $3,299, and when configured, the pre-tax price can reach $3,600. As a result, a gap has opened up in the market for other manufacturers to offer larger Retina-class displays for Mac users, and the new Meirro Pro is designed to fill exactly that gap. The Meirro Pro is a 32-inch 6K display with an all-aluminum body, single-cable connectivity, and an adjustable stand, all for just $1,199. I've been using it as my daily main monitor for a while now, and although Meirro has made some compromises to hit that price, it remains the most convincing Studio Display alternative I've tested. Here's everything you need to know.

Don't miss our hands-on Meirro Pro video for a first-hand look!

Design and Specifications

The first thing that strikes you is just how similar it looks to the current Apple Studio Display. This monitor fits naturally into any Apple desktop setup without any違和感. It's built entirely from CNC-machined aluminum and comes with the same adjustable stand, giving it a truly premium feel. The build quality adds a sense of solidity to any desk. Most non-Apple displays use plastic housings, and their stands tend to be flimsy and unstable, but you'll find no plastic components anywhere on the Meirro Pro.

Unboxing and setup are equally straightforward. Attach the base to the stand, fix the stand to the back of the monitor, plug in the power, and it turns on. The design is minimalist with no buttons at all, and the power supply is built into the body. That means no bulky external power brick cluttering up your desk. The monitor ships with an adjustable stand and a VESA mount adapter at no extra cost. The overall look and styling once again give off a strong Apple vibe—which is exactly what I was after.

But how does the actual display perform? As mentioned at the outset, this is a true 6K panel. It uses a 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel with a resolution of 6144 × 3456, equivalent to 224 ppi, delivering Retina-class sharpness. Here are the key specs:

  • 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel
  • 6144 × 3456 resolution
  • 224 PPI
  • 60Hz refresh rate
  • 2,000:1 contrast ratio
  • 10-bit color, supporting over 1.07 billion colors
  • 98% DCI-P3 color gamut
  • 99.5% Adobe RGB color gamut
  • Typical brightness of 450 nits, HDR peak brightness of 750 nits

The panel also comes with a glossy anti-reflective coating, which is the only option available. While I'd love to have a matte option as well, even in a room with plenty of window light, the glossy finish still performs admirably.

Ports and Accessories

Like Apple's displays, the Meirro Pro offers a total of five USB-C ports on the back as its only I/O, keeping things nicely minimal. One of these serves as the primary upstream connection, supporting DisplayPort 2.1, up to 80Gbps bandwidth, and up to 96W of power delivery, ensuring your MacBook stays fully charged at all times. That means a single cable carries the 6K video signal. The remaining four USB-C ports are downstream, but their data transfer speeds are fairly limited—all USB 2.0. They're still more than adequate for connecting webcams, speakers, and other peripherals.

Since the Meirro Pro has no buttons at all (not even a power button), it ships with a remote that looks very similar to the previous-generation Apple TV remote. The remote has a power button and lets you access the display's system settings when needed.

Usage Experience and Setup

I've set up the Meirro Pro as the sole main display on my desk, and the experience has been excellent. The 32-inch size combined with 6K resolution delivers—both in physical space and pixel density—exactly what I've been looking for in a high-end Mac display.

My setup is simple. I frequently use external SSDs and like connecting through a Satechi Thunderbolt hub, so I run the display through that hub. One Thunderbolt cable goes from the display to the hub, and another goes from the hub to my MacBook Pro. Everything works exactly as expected.

I tested it across all my daily workflows, and the Meirro Pro handled them with ease. I edited in Final Cut Pro, organized various media files, and the extra screen real estate was a huge help. My work also involves a lot of research, often requiring many tabs and windows open at once; the additional pixel density makes the screen feel even wider than 32 inches. The most important feature of this display is its 224 PPI, which allows macOS—and even iPadOS—to scale correctly as Apple intended.

One last point worth mentioning is that the solid build quality effectively reduces wobble. Most similar displays I've used shake when I type, especially when I'm using a standing desk. The Meirro Pro's materials and sturdy stand work together to significantly reduce wobble. So, whether you're looking at the specs or the real-world experience, the Meirro Pro is a strong alternative to the Studio Display. That said, at this price point, there are some compromises worth noting.

Compromises

A 32-inch 6K display with a fully CNC-machined aluminum body for under $1,200 sounds almost too good to be true. To hit that price, Meirro has had to make some trade-offs. Since most potential buyers will compare it to the Studio Display, it's worth noting that it lacks the following features. The Meirro Pro does not include or support:

  • Built-in webcam
  • Speakers
  • Microphone
  • No daisy-chaining support

Personally, these compromises are worth it, because I already own an external webcam and speakers. The lack of a microphone doesn't bother me either, since I use AirPods or a Shure mic whenever needed. I just want anyone considering this purchase to be fully aware of these differences.

The last trade-off I noticed is the speed of the USB-C ports on the back of the display. The Apple Studio Display offers four USB-C ports in total—two of which are Thunderbolt, and two at USB 3.0 speeds. The Meirro Pro, while offering more USB-C ports overall, only has one Thunderbolt port; the other four are noticeably slower at USB 2.0. This doesn't affect me much, since I already have a Satechi Thunderbolt dock, but I understand some users might need faster transfer speeds.

However, even with these trade-offs in mind, I still believe the Meirro Pro is, without question, my top recommendation over the Apple Studio Display, because the value it delivers is simply unmatched.

Pricing and Availability

The Meirro Pro is priced at $1,299 standard, and is currently available for pre-order at $1,199, with shipping expected to begin on August 1. If you already have a monitor arm, you can choose the version without the stand and save $50, bringing the total down to $1,149. The $1,199 price includes:

  • Meirro Pro display
  • Aluminum stand
  • VESA mount adapter
  • USB-C cable
  • Power cable
  • Remote control

Conclusion

The Meirro Pro is the best true Studio Display alternative I've tested. For just $1,199, you get a 32-inch 6K display with Retina-class sharpness, a glossy Nano IPS Black panel, an all-aluminum body, single-cable Mac connectivity, an adjustable stand, and a VESA mount adapter. If you're after Apple's most complete all-in-one desktop experience, the Studio Display still has its advantages; but if you already have some external accessories and prioritize screen size, resolution, build quality, and value, the Meirro Pro is absolutely worth recommending.

What do you think? Is this a monitor you'd consider picking up? Do you already own a Studio Display? Do you miss the Pro Display XDR? I'd love to hear your thoughts. And again, don't miss our hands-on video so you can see it in action!
